Prescribing information
Evidence

Clinical evidence for olanzapine

Reviewing clinical outcomes in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The clinical evidence for olanzapine includes studies of symptom improvement in schizophrenia, treatment of manic episodes and prevention of recurrence in bipolar disorder.

Evidence should be considered in the context of the indication, patient population, comparator, endpoint and duration of follow-up. Individual study results do not necessarily predict the response of every patient.

Schizophrenia

Evidence in schizophrenia

The European SmPC summarises placebo-controlled and comparator-controlled studies in patients with schizophrenia.

In two of two placebo-controlled studies and two of three comparator-controlled studies described in the SmPC, involving over 2,900 patients presenting with both positive and negative symptoms, olanzapine was associated with statistically significantly greater improvement in negative as well as positive symptoms.1

The SmPC also summarises a multinational, double-blind comparative study involving 1,481 patients with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder and related disorders who had varying degrees of depressive symptoms. A prospective secondary analysis of changes in mood scores favoured olanzapine over haloperidol.1

This was a secondary analysis and was not the primary outcome of the study.

Published trial · Schizophrenia

Olanzapine versus placebo and haloperidol: North American double-blind trial

A 6-week, randomised, double-blind trial in 335 patients with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia compared three olanzapine dose ranges with haloperidol and placebo. In overall symptoms (BPRS total), the medium and high olanzapine ranges and haloperidol were superior to placebo. In negative symptoms (SANS composite), the low and high olanzapine ranges were superior to placebo, and the high range was also superior to haloperidol.10

Design
Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled; 22 sites, US and Canada
Patients
n = 335; DSM-III-R schizophrenia, acute exacerbation; BPRS total ≥ 24; about 91% chronic course
Arms
Olanzapine 5 ± 2.5, 10 ± 2.5 or 15 ± 2.5 mg/day; haloperidol 15 ± 5 mg/day; placebo
Endpoints
Primary objectives: change in BPRS total and BPRS positive versus placebo; SANS composite versus placebo and haloperidol (LOCF)

Safety in this trial

Somnolence was reported in 39.1% of patients on the high olanzapine range versus 16.2% on placebo. Mean weight gain at endpoint was 3.5 kg on the high range. Dose-related transaminase elevations occurred, and six olanzapine-treated patients discontinued because of raised ALT without clinical signs of hepatic dysfunction. No acute dystonia occurred with olanzapine (13.0% with haloperidol).10

Limitations. Six-week acute phase; high placebo response; the haloperidol comparator dose (mean modal 16.4 mg/day) has been discussed as higher than optimal, which may favour comparisons against it.10,8

Bipolar disorder

Evidence in acute mania

The product information describes clinical studies evaluating olanzapine in acute manic or mixed episodes associated with bipolar disorder.

The SmPC does not report effect sizes for these studies. Outcomes are therefore given in words.

  • Comparison with placebo

    Superior efficacy to placebo in reduction of manic symptoms over 3 weeks.1

  • Comparison with divalproex

    Superior efficacy to valproate semisodium (divalproex) in reduction of manic symptoms over 3 weeks.1

  • Combination with lithium or valproate

    Adding olanzapine 10 mg to lithium or valproate resulted in a greater reduction in symptoms of mania than lithium or valproate monotherapy after 6 weeks.1

  • Symptomatic remission

    Comparable efficacy results to haloperidol in the proportion of patients in symptomatic remission from mania and depression at 6 and 12 weeks.1

Published trial · Acute mania

Olanzapine versus placebo in the treatment of acute mania

A 3-week, randomised, double-blind trial in 139 patients with a manic or mixed episode of bipolar I disorder. Olanzapine produced a significantly greater mean improvement in Young Mania Rating Scale total score than placebo (primary endpoint), and significantly more patients met the predefined response criterion.11

Design
Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group; 16 US sites
Patients
n = 139 (olanzapine 70, placebo 69); DSM-IV bipolar disorder, manic or mixed episode; YMRS ≥ 20; 53% with psychotic features
Dosing
Olanzapine started at 10 mg/day, adjustable 5–20 mg/day; mean modal dose 14.9 mg/day
Endpoints
Primary: change in YMRS total (LOCF). Response defined a priori as ≥ 50% YMRS decrease

Safety in this trial

Somnolence (32.9% vs 17.4%), dry mouth (25.7% vs 8.7%), dizziness (22.9% vs 5.8%) and weight gain (11.4% vs 1.4%) were more frequent with olanzapine. Mean weight change was +1.65 kg versus −0.44 kg over 3 weeks. Treatment-emergent ALT elevations occurred in 17.6% of olanzapine-treated patients versus 0% on placebo.11

Limitations. Three-week duration; high placebo dropout (65.2%); concomitant lorazepam permitted. The EU SmPC recommends a 15 mg starting dose for monotherapy of a manic episode, whereas this trial started at 10 mg.11,1

Bipolar disorder

Evidence in recurrence prevention

Clinical studies have evaluated continued olanzapine treatment in patients who responded to treatment for a manic episode.

The European SmPC reports statistically significant superiority over placebo in a 12-month recurrence-prevention study. It also describes a second study comparing olanzapine with lithium after remission achieved with combination treatment, in which olanzapine was statistically non-inferior.1

In an 18-month study, olanzapine co-therapy with lithium or valproate was not statistically significantly superior to lithium or valproate alone in delaying recurrence.1

Safety over time

Long-term treatment considerations

Long-term treatment requires evaluation of both clinical response and safety.

The product information notes that the proportion of adult patients with clinically significant changes in weight, glucose, total/LDL/HDL cholesterol or triglycerides increased over time with longer exposure (at least 48 weeks). Ongoing monitoring is therefore an important part of treatment.1

The available evidence should be presented in a balanced manner, including relevant limitations, adverse effects and the distinction between trial findings and real-world observations.

Monitoring recommendations
Context

Guideline and formulary context

Treatment guidelines place olanzapine among several options, not ahead of them. Their recommendations depend on the phase of illness, the patient's preferences and how well the adverse-effect profile suits that person. Local guidance and reimbursement rules apply.

Summary of guideline and formulary positions relevant to olanzapine
SourceScopeRelevant statements
APA practice guideline, 3rd ed., 20216SchizophreniaTreat with an antipsychotic and monitor effectiveness and side effects (1A). Continue antipsychotic treatment after symptoms improve (1A), preferably with the same medication (2B). Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (1B). Long-acting injectable if the patient prefers it or adherence is poor (2B). The guideline does not rank individual antipsychotics.
BAP guidelines, 20167Bipolar disorderFor severe mania, consider an oral dopamine antagonist; haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone and quetiapine are described as particularly effective. In long-term treatment, olanzapine is among the agents shown to prevent manic relapse; lithium is recommended as initial monotherapy. Weight gain is noted as a prominent adverse effect of olanzapine.
WPA review, 20088SchizophreniaApart from clozapine, no consistent efficacy differences between second-generation antipsychotics. Olanzapine is associated with more weight gain and metabolic adverse effects than most comparators.
WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 20239Psychotic and bipolar disordersOlanzapine is listed as a therapeutic alternative to risperidone for psychotic disorders and to quetiapine for bipolar disorders.
